cards.title: Masumi Yamada
cards.sub: 2015 · Disaster Prevention Research Institute, Kyoto University
cards.prompt: The fix for the 2011 false alarms added no sensors and did not lengthen the wait. Yamada and three co-authors rewrote one step of the pipeline. Which step, and what second measurement did they feed it so it could tell one large earthquake from two small ones?
cards.answer: The association step: deciding which event each P-wave pick belongs to. They made it probabilistic, treating the number of concurrent earthquakes as something to infer rather than assume, and fed it maximum displacement amplitude alongside P-wave picking times, because a station close to a real epicentre should not be reading small. JMA's IPF, running since 2016, rests on the same Bayesian inference and cites this paper for it.
cards.body: Masumi Yamada, at Kyoto University's Disaster Prevention Research Institute. With S. Wu and J. L. Beck at Caltech and Koji Tamaribuchi at JMA, she worked the 2011 sequence backwards. The picks were real arrivals. What had failed was the step that decides which earthquake each pick belongs to.

cards.title: The two months after Tohoku
cards.prompt: In the two months after the main shock, JMA's public warnings were wrong more often than they were right. How many of the 70 were inappropriate, and what share of those came from the concurrent-event problem rather than from broken sensors?
cards.answer: 44 of the 70 were inappropriate, misses and false alarms counted together. Over 70 per cent of the 44 were caused by multiple concurrent events.
cards.body: Japan's early warning system had just done the thing it was built for: an early warning on 11 March, before the S-wave reached anywhere in the country. Then the aftershock sequence began, several earthquakes at a time, and warnings went out for shaking that never came, while some that mattered never went out at all.

cards.title: Wu, Yamada, Tamaribuchi and Beck
cards.prompt: This paper states, in one sentence, how two earthquakes become one inside the JMA pipeline. Reproduce it using the terms 'near source' and 'far source', and name the quantity it corrupts and the direction of the error.
cards.answer: Some of the near source stations of the second event were treated as far source stations of the first. Distance is inferred from arrival time, so a strong nearby reading is priced as a weak distant one. That corrupts the magnitude estimate, and the error runs upward, which is why the result is a false alarm rather than a miss.
cards.body: 'Multi-events earthquake early warning algorithm using a Bayesian approach', doi 10.1093/gji/ggu437, online 11 December 2014. Eighteen pages of Bayesian model selection whose first question is not where the earthquake is but how many earthquakes there are. Tamaribuchi is at JMA, so the operator co-authored the count of its own failures.

cards.title: IPF, and the January that repeated it
cards.prompt: JMA shipped the multi-event fix and then hit the same wall. What did the January 2018 pair of earthquakes do that IPF was built to prevent, and what does that force you to build into any pipeline allowed to close a window early?
cards.answer: Two earthquakes about 400 km apart happened at the same time, and the system computed the M4.5's magnitude from the M4.0's displacement amplitudes, overpredicting the shaking. IPF located both events correctly; the event-identification step after it associated them wrongly. A smarter cutoff narrows the failure, it never removes it, so anything that closes a window early also needs a way to correct and retract the result afterwards.
cards.body: IPF entered JMA operation on 14 December 2016, weighing amplitude as well as travel-time difference before it associates a pick. PLUM followed on 22 March 2018, predicting shaking directly from ground motion observed near the target instead of from a source estimate. 150 S-net ocean-bottom seismometers were added in 2019 and 2020.
